subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Unit 4 Personal Or Creative Writing And Reading Literary And Non Fiction Texts
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the assessment objectives.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which sentence is the strongest, most memorable ending to a persuasive piece?
options: So yeah, that's about it really.
That is the end of my writing.
I think I have said enough now.
The choice is yours: act now, or watch our future slip away.
questions.explain: A direct, balanced final appeal leaves a lasting impression on the reader.

questions.q: A story is told using "I crept down the stairs, my heart pounding." What narrative perspective is this?
options: Third-person limited
Third-person omniscient
Second-person
First-person
questions.explain: The pronoun "I" signals a first-person narrator telling their own experience.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a writer SHOWING rather than TELLING emotion?
options: "She bit her nails and glanced at the door again and again."
"She felt anxiety."
"She was scared, the text says."
"She was very nervous."
questions.explain: Describing actions (nail-biting, glancing) lets the reader infer nervousness, which is "showing."

questions.q: What is the reader most likely meant to FEEL from: "The orphan watched the other children open their gifts, his own hands empty"?
options: Sympathy for the orphan
Anger at the orphan
Boredom
Amusement
questions.explain: The image of the empty-handed orphan beside happy children is designed to evoke sympathy.

questions.q: When an extract suddenly shifts focus from a wide view of a crowd to one trembling child, this structural technique:
options: Changes the narrator to second person
Removes all tension
Ends the narrative
Narrows the focus to direct the reader's attention
questions.explain: Moving from the general to a single detail is a deliberate narrowing of focus that guides reader attention.

questions.q: Which sentence best uses 'show, not tell' to convey that a character is nervous?
options: She felt nervous and scared inside.
Her hands trembled as she gripped the pencil, her eyes fixed on the clock.
The girl was nervous because of the test.
She was very nervous about the exam.
questions.explain: Showing physical detail lets the reader infer the emotion rather than stating it outright.

questions.q: Which sentence opener creates the most engaging, dramatic story opening?
options: It was a normal day at school.
The door slammed shut behind me, and the lights went out.
My name is Tom and this is my story.
I am going to tell you about a time I was scared.
questions.explain: Starting in the middle of the action (in medias res) hooks the reader immediately.

questions.q: A writer ends a story by returning to the same rainy street where it began. This ending technique is best called:
options: Flashback
Cyclical structure
Cliffhanger
Foreshadowing
questions.explain: Returning to the opening situation creates a cyclical (circular) structure.

questions.q: You are writing a speech. Which feature would make it most engaging for a live audience?
options: Footnotes and references
Long, unbroken paragraphs of dense detail
A bulleted shopping list
A repeated phrase used as a rallying refrain
questions.explain: Repetition (anaphora) builds rhythm and impact, ideal for spoken delivery.

questions.q: You are writing a leaflet for a local charity event. Which feature is most appropriate to the form?
options: A single dense block of text
Footnotes and academic citations
Clear headings, bullet points and key details like time and place
No headings at all
questions.explain: Leaflets use headings, bullets and signposting so readers can scan key information quickly.

questions.q: An exam asks: "How does the writer use language to create a sense of fear?" What should your answer focus on?
options: Retelling the plot of the extract
The author's biography
How long the extract is
Specific words and phrases and the effects they create
questions.explain: A "how does the writer use language" question requires analysis of word choices and their effects, not plot summary.

questions.q: An extract opens with a long, calm description of a sunny garden, then a single line: "Then the screaming began." What is the structural effect of this shift?
options: It signals the end of the story
It creates a jarring contrast that shocks the reader
It tells us the setting is unimportant
It makes the passage boring
questions.explain: The sudden shift from calm to violence creates contrast and shock, a deliberate structural effect.
